description: The deterministic projection from the selected XNA contract to Common Lisp. tools/api-compat/verify.py applies these rules to the live image; docs/common-lisp-mapping.md is the prose that explains them.

naming.identifier: A CLR identifier becomes a Lisp symbol by inserting a hyphen at each case boundary and lowercasing. Texture2D becomes texture-2d, because the D after the digit starts a new word; Bgra4444 becomes bgra4444, because nothing does. That is the same rule the generated ABI constants already follow.
naming.reference_type_member: <member>, in the type's package, as a generic function or reader.
naming.value_type_member: <type>-<member>, in the type's package. The prefix is what keeps Rectangle's Left from colliding with Viewport's.
naming.static_class_member: <class>-<member>, so that Mouse and GamePad can join Keyboard's namespace without collision.
naming.constructor: make-instance for a reference type; make-<type> for a value type.
naming.enum_member: a keyword named by the identifier rule; the exact value is preserved in the runtime table.

OnExiting(Object,EventArgs).reason: The CLR event-handler pattern passes a sender and an argument object. A CLOS method on the game needs neither: the game is the receiver, and the exiting notification carries nothing else.

Components.reason: The game's one collection, answered by identity because XNA's is a field.

LaunchParameters.reason: Answered by identity, as XNA's field is. CNA has no route that reports a game's launch parameters, so it is empty unless the program fills it -- recorded in docs/limitations.md rather than left to be discovered.

Content.reason: The game's own content manager, answered by identity because XNA's is a field. Read-only, and the missing setter is deliberate: XNA's Game.Content = m assigns a reference, and CNA's cna_game_set_content_manager_ext *copies* -- its own header says "the canonical setter takes a reference and copies, so this does too: the caller keeps its own manager". Reading the property back would therefore answer a different object than the one assigned, so the member is reported partial rather than projected as something that silently means something else. docs/limitations.md.

not_applicable.Dispose(Boolean): The protected dispose(bool disposing) pattern exists to tell a finalizer call from an explicit one. CNA-Lisp has no finalizer that touches a native resource, so there is nothing for the flag to distinguish.

unimplemented.Services: GameServiceContainer, which CNA does not have a container for. It has cna_game_services_contains_ext and remove_ext over a closed CNA_GAME_SERVICE_TYPE_* enum and no route that registers a service or hands one back, so GetService -- the member the type exists for -- cannot be answered for the two services the runtime registers. Not, as an earlier note claimed, because IGraphicsDeviceService is unprojectable: its five members are already complete on GraphicsDeviceManager, the type that implements it. docs/limitations.md carries the audit.

Activated.reason: A CLR event is two operations, add_E and remove_E, and it projects to two generic functions on the object that raises it. They are generic because Disposed is raised by more than one type in this package and a plain function could not be specialised on the second. The handler takes the sender and nothing else: EventArgs.Empty carries no information, and a second always-empty argument would be something every handler had to write and ignore.

unimplemented.new(): XNA's constructor is public and a standalone collection is legal there, if useless -- a Game makes its own and drives that one. CNA has no route for a collection apart from a game's: `a game owns exactly one component collection, so the collection needs no handle of its own and every route addresses the game's`. So a standalone one is not projected rather than faked.

GameComponent.reason: The one event argument in this binding that is not empty. Every other CLR event in the selection carries EventArgs.Empty and its handlers take the sender alone; these two carry the component, so their handlers take the sender and this object.

DeviceCreated.reason: The same projection Game's events use, over cna_graphics_device_manager_subscribe. CNA gives manager registrations the same handle type and the same release route as the game's, so one mechanism serves both.

unimplemented.PreparingDeviceSettings: The only event in the selection that carries data. It needs PreparingDeviceSettingsEventArgs and GraphicsDeviceInformation, neither of which is in the selection, and CNA's non-ext callback for it can only observe the settings where XNA's event exists to change them. Projecting the observing form under the event's name would be a quieter kind of wrong than leaving it missing.

Load(String).reason: Load<T> is generic over the asset type, and this is the one place the projection is closer to XNA than the C ABI can be: CNA spells the generic method as one route per asset type -- cna_content_manager_load_texture2d, _load_sprite_font, _load_texture_cube -- because a C caller cannot name a type. Common Lisp can, so the type stays an argument and Load<T> stays one member. Reported partial: the three types above are the ones CNA has a route for, and LOADABLE-ASSET-TYPES answers which.

Unload().reason: Read from the pinned IL: Unload throws ObjectDisposedException when loadedAssets is already null, walks disposableAssets calling IDisposable.Dispose on every entry, and clears both collections in a finally. All three are reproduced. The manager keeps XNA's two collections -- a name-keyed cache and a disposal list -- so it has assets of its own to release, and Unload releases them: a SpriteFont before the atlas it keeps alive, and a later asset before an earlier one. CNA's cna_content_manager_unload is called as well, so neither side is left holding an asset the other has let go. **One deliberate divergence, and it is documented:** XNA's Unload has no error handling, so a throwing Dispose stops it while the finally still clears both collections -- which strands every remaining asset with nothing left that can reach it. There are no finalizers here by policy, so reproducing that would leak permanently and fail the game's teardown; this releases every independent asset and then signals the first failure. docs/limitations.md.

Dispose().reason: XNA's Dispose() is Dispose(true) followed by GC.SuppressFinalize, and Dispose(bool) is Unload() and then nulling both collections -- a purely managed operation that destroys nothing native. That is what happens here, for **both** kinds of manager. A game's own manager is disposable: it unloads its assets and is marked disposed, and the borrowed native manager CNA says "cannot be destroyed" is left alone, which is no loss because XNA has nothing native to destroy either. Game.Content keeps answering the disposed manager afterwards, as XNA's field does, and every member on it then refuses -- ObjectDisposedException on that side, CNA-DISPOSED-ERROR on this one. A manager this binding created additionally destroys its native object, which is the one thing XNA has no counterpart for because it has no native object.

Multiply.reason: One projection; the operator and the named method are the same operation.

.ctor.reason: XNA tells the integer and float constructors apart by static type, and Common Lisp would have to tell 1 from 1.0 at run time to do the same. Those two mean almost opposite colours -- (make-color 1 1 1) is very nearly black where (make-color-from-floats 1.0 1.0 1.0) is white -- so the distinction is a name here rather than a numeric type nobody can see. The Vector3 and Vector4 forms are named for the same reason, and their arity would not separate them anyway.

FromNonPremultiplied.reason: The two overloads are different computations, not one operation reached two ways: the integer form truncates an integer quotient and the Vector4 form multiplies in floats and packs through PackUNorm. They disagree by a level on ordinary inputs, so collapsing them would hide a real difference.

Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Color.predefined_value_reason: XNA's 141 predefined colours are static properties on a value type. They are reached here by keyword through PREDEFINED-COLOR, which the generated table makes exhaustive; the thirteen with a named function of their own are declared extensions. A Lisp constant would be wrong for all of them, because Color is mutable and every read of the original is a copy.

OpenStream(String).reason: **Partial, and the reasons are exact.** The path validation is XNA's own, transcribed from the assembly rather than delegated: GetCleanPath's slash folding, `.\` stripping, `\.\` collapsing and left-to-right `\..\` resolution, then IsCleanPathAbsolute's refusals -- a rooted path, a leading or trailing `..`, an embedded `\..\`, and the seven characters its badCharacters array holds, read out of the assembly's static data blob (3A 00 2A 00 3F 00 22 00 3C 00 3E 00 7C 00) rather than guessed. So `a/../b` resolves to `b` and is accepted and `../b` is refused, on both sides. The stream is a real, lazily-read Common Lisp binary input stream over the file, which is what XNA's File.OpenRead answers; CNA's cna_title_container_read_ext is deliberately not used, because its own header calls itself a narrowing -- "This ABI has no stream handle for title content ... incremental reads over a title stream are not available" -- and taking it would make this member less like XNA than the language already allows. The base path does come from CNA, through cna_title_location_copy_path, so an override made there is honoured. Two things are not reproduced, and they are why this is partial rather than complete. XNA round-trips the cleaned name through `new Uri(name, UriKind.Relative)` and turns any exception into an ArgumentException; no input that survives the checks above has been found to fail that construction, but this binding cannot evidence that it rejects nothing, so it is not claimed to. And XNA's member is static and needs no game, while CNA's title-location routes take a game handle for thread affinity -- so this needs the process's one active game, exactly as Keyboard.GetState does. docs/limitations.md.
